Situation1: They send an occasional text to check in with their parents over the weekend.
Expectation2: Support individuals or groups in accessing essential services and resources
Situation2: They assist someone who is struggling with paperwork or procedures needed to receive public support.
Story: My phone buzzed with a message from Mom: “Hope you’re having a good weekend. Call us when you can.” I glanced at the clock—already past noon on Sunday. I hadn’t called home all week, just sent a quick text yesterday. Guilt pricked at me; I knew how much my parents valued hearing my voice, especially since Dad’s health scare last month. But right now, I was sitting across from Mrs. Ramirez at the community center, her hands trembling as she tried to fill out the forms for housing assistance. She looked at me, eyes pleading for help, and I knew how much she depended on me to guide her through this maze of paperwork. My mind tugged in two directions: the son who should call home, reassure his parents, and the advocate who couldn’t abandon someone in need. I felt the weight of both roles pressing on me, each demanding my time, my care, my presence. My phone vibrated again. I stared at it, heart pounding, torn between the family I came from and the people I promised to help.
